questions.question: In a compare and contrast essay, what is the "block method"?
options: Describing one subject completely first, then the other
Comparing the subjects aspect by aspect
Writing only about similarities
Writing only about differences
questions.explanation: The block method covers all aspects of subject A first, then subject B. The point-by-point method compares them aspect by aspect.

questions.question: When is the point-by-point method usually the better choice?
options: For longer texts and thorough analyses
For very short and simple comparisons
When you only have one subject
When you want to avoid structure
questions.explanation: Point-by-point works best for longer texts and deep analyses, while the block method suits short, simple comparisons.

questions.question: Which phrase signals a SIMILARITY?
options: Similarly,
In contrast,
However,
Whereas
questions.explanation: "Similarly", "likewise" and "in the same way" signal similarities. "In contrast", "however" and "whereas" signal differences.

questions.question: Which sentence uses contrast language correctly?
options: Whereas London is huge, Oslo is a fairly small capital.
Whereas London is huge, and Oslo too.
Similarly, London is huge but Oslo is small.
Both London is huge and Oslo is small.
questions.explanation: "Whereas" links two contrasting facts: "Whereas A is..., B is...". "Similarly" would wrongly signal a similarity here.

questions.question: What should the conclusion of a compare and contrast essay do?
options: Sum up the main similarities and differences and give a final insight
Introduce a completely new subject
Repeat the whole essay word for word
List sources only
questions.explanation: The conclusion summarises the key similarities and differences and often offers a final evaluation or insight.
